question:
A 50-year-old woman comes to the clinic with a one-month history of low back pain. She denies any
recent trauma and works as a journalist, spending most of her time seated at a desk. On examination
in the prone position, there is a deep sacral sulcus on the right and a posterior inferior lateral angle
(ILA) on the left. During a seated forward bend test, the left posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) moves
superiorly. L5 is noted to be flexed, rotated to the right, and sidebent to the right. What is the most likely
diagnosis? Answer Choices: (A) left-on-left sacral torsion (B) right-on-left sacral torsion (C) bilateral
sacral flexion (D) unilateral sacral flexion on the right (E) unilateral sacral extension on the left (F)
left-on-right sacral torsion (G) bilateral sacral extension (H) sacral shear dysfunction on the right (I)
anterior sacral base dysfunction (J) right-on-right sacral torsion
 A. right-on-left sacral torsion
B. bilateral sacral flexion
C. unilateral sacral flexion on the right
D. sacral shear dysfunction on the right
E. left-on-left sacral torsion
F. bilateral sacral extension
G. unilateral sacral extension on the left
H. left-on-right sacral torsion
I. anterior sacral base dysfunction
J. right-on-right sacral torsion
